content_html:
An account balance tells you how many dollars you will have, not what those dollars will buy. This calculator projects an investment's balance, then strips out inflation to show its value in today's money and the real rate of return you earned after rising prices are taken into account.

How to use this calculator

  1. Starting amount and yearly contribution: what you invest now and what you plan to add each year. Either can be 0, but not both.
  2. Annual return (nominal): the yearly rate before inflation, such as a quoted interest rate or an assumed average investment return.
  3. Annual inflation rate: how fast you expect prices to rise on average. Test a few rates, since inflation varies from year to year.
  4. Years and compounding: how long the money stays invested and how often the return is credited.
  5. More options: add contributions at the start or end of each year, and keep them fixed or raise them each year with inflation so they keep the same buying power.

Nominal vs real returns

The nominal balance grows by (1 + r/n)n each year, where r is the annual return and n the number of compounding periods. To express a future balance in today's dollars, divide it by the rise in prices over the same period: real value = nominal value ÷ (1 + inflation)years.

The real rate of return follows the same logic. It is (1 + nominal rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1, which is a little lower than simply subtracting inflation from the return. At 7% and 3% the shortcut says 4%, while the exact figure is 3.88%. The gap grows when both rates are high.

Worked example

Using the default inputs, you start with $10,000 and add $1,200 at the start of each year for 20 years, earning 7% a year compounded monthly (an effective 7.23% a year) while prices rise 3% a year.

ResultAmount
Total contributed$34,000.00
Ending balance (nominal)$94,476.30
Value in today's dollars$52,309.23
Inflation cost$42,167.06
Real annual return4.11%

After 20 years of 3% inflation, a dollar buys about 55 cents' worth of today's goods, so the $94,476.30 balance has roughly the spending power of $52,309.23 now. That is still well above the $34,000 contributed, because the 7.23% return comfortably beats inflation.

Practical tips

  • Plan in today's dollars. A retirement or savings target set in today's money is easier to picture, and the real balance tells you whether you are on track.
  • Raise contributions with inflation if you can. A fixed $1,200 is worth less every year, and indexing it keeps your saving effort constant in real terms.
  • Cash that earns less than inflation loses buying power even though its balance rises. The real return turns negative whenever inflation is higher than the nominal rate.
  • Taxes and fees reduce the return you actually keep, so the real return after costs is usually lower than shown here.

faq.question: What is an inflation-adjusted return?
faq.answer: It is the return on an investment after accounting for rising prices, also called the real return. It shows how much your purchasing power grew, rather than how many more dollars you have.

faq.question: Why not just subtract inflation from my return?
faq.answer: Subtracting is a close approximation when rates are low, but the exact real return divides one plus the nominal return by one plus inflation. The difference is small at low rates and grows when returns and inflation are both high.

faq.question: What inflation rate should I use?
faq.answer: Use the average rate you expect over the whole period, not the latest monthly reading. Because the future is uncertain, it helps to run a low, middle and high inflation rate and compare the results.

faq.question: Can the real return be negative?
faq.answer: Yes. Whenever inflation is higher than your nominal return, your balance still grows in dollars but buys less each year, and the calculator shows a negative real return.

faq.question: Does the calculator include taxes or fees?
faq.answer: No. Results are before taxes and investment costs. If you want to allow for them, lower the annual return you enter by roughly the yearly fees and taxes you expect to pay.
